text: You have a sorted array of distinct integers, but it was rotated at some unknown point. For example, zero through seven might come to you as four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two. Find the index of a target, or return minus one. It has to run in log time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the array was sorted going up, then rotated exactly once, and all the values are different. Is that right?
Can the rotation be zero — that is, can I get a plain sorted array with nothing moved?
Good — I'll make sure my code handles it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to five thousand elements, values within about ten thousand either way.

Let me say the hard part out loud first, because it changes the whole approach. Normally binary search works because one yes or no test is monotonic along the array. Here that breaks. Take four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two, and ask: is this value at least five? The answers go false, true, true, true, false, false, false. It turns true and then turns false again. So if I land in the middle and see a false, I can't tell whether to go left or right. Plain lower bound is off the table.

But something is still true. Rotating a sorted array creates exactly one break point — the one spot where the value drops. If I cut the range at the middle, that single break can only sit in one of the two halves. So the other half is always fully sorted. That's the piece I can trust, and I'll build the search on it.

Let me run through the example, looking for zero. The middle is seven, at index three. The left side, four through seven, is clean and rising, so that's my trusted half. Is zero between four and seven? No. So it can't be on the left at all, and I throw away four cells in one step.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to just scan every cell. Correct, but linear time, and the problem asks for log time. This problem reminds me of ordinary binary search with one extra question in front. There are two ways to go. One: find the break point first with its own binary search, then run a normal search on whichever piece the target belongs to. Two: do it in a single pass, deciding each round which half is sorted. Both are log time. I'll do the single pass, since it's one loop. I'll mention the two-step version as the easier-to-debug option.

Here's the plan. One: keep a closed range and shrink it to one cell. Two: each round, ask which half is sorted, and whether the target sits inside that half's range, and go that way or the other. Three: check that last cell against the target. One thing worth flagging — the range check and the shrink have to agree about mid. On the left-sorted branch I set right to mid, so mid stays a candidate and the range test must include it. On the right-sorted branch I set left to mid plus one, so mid is stepped over and the test must exclude it — otherwise a target sitting exactly on mid gets skipped. The trade-off: four branches make it easy to flip a sign; the two-step version is safer but costs two searches. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop that shrinks to a single cell. If nums at left is at most nums at mid, the left half is sorted, and I move into it or past it; otherwise the right half is sorted, with the mirror moves. After the loop, I return left only if that cell equals the target. One thing worth flagging — the less-or-equal in that first test. With two cells left, mid equals left, and a single cell must count as sorted. With a strict less-than, the code calls the right half sorted and shrinks the wrong way: two, zero, looking for zero, returns minus one instead of one.

Let's dry-run the code. Four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two, target zero — I expect index four. The row that matters is the last one: two cells left, so mid is left, and that less-or-equal makes the single cell zero the sorted half. The target is in it, right comes down to four, and the check outside confirms nums at four is zero. So I return four. Corner cases: a missing target returns minus one, since the loop only eliminates — that's why the final check isn't optional. Five, six, seven, zero, one, two, four, looking for six, takes the right-sorted branch and returns one. No rotation works normally, and a single cell skips the loop. I also brute-forced six hundred sixty cases, all passing.

The time complexity is log n. All four branches cut the range in half, so the extra question is just a constant — two or three comparisons per round instead of one. The space complexity is constant. In the worst-case scenario it's about thirteen rounds at five thousand elements, same as a plain binary search. Oh, one more thing — this leans hard on the values being distinct. With duplicates, when nums at left equals nums at mid, you can't tell a flat run from one that hides the break. Zero, one, zero, zero, zero, looking for one, would return minus one. The fix is a third branch that just moves left forward by one, which is safe but drops the worst case to linear time.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You showed why plain binary search fails here by writing out the broken true and false pattern, instead of just asserting it. You reduced the whole problem to one fact — a single break point can only ruin one half — and built the loop on that. And you tied the range check's open and closed ends to the shrink direction, with the smallest input that breaks the sorted-half test. Good work.
